newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FEATURE - Plane crash fears cloud African skies.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Plane crash fears cloud African skies.

text.p: Pilots say flying over Africa is like playing Russian roulette -- taking your life in your hands and just a matter of time before there's a bang.
Flights over Africa have surged 120 percent over the past five years and airline pilots worldwide say the continent is en route to a major air disaster.
Virtually non-existent air traffic control is to blame.
Conference after conference urges a drastic solution before hundreds of airline passengers are killed in a crash.

"There is just no time for the 'five-year plan' type solution to the critical problems in Africa," Tony van Heerden, past president of the Air Line Pilots' Association of South Africa (ALPA-SA), said last October.
"You may believe that I am being unduly pessimistic, but I assure you, that is not so. It is a jungle out there," he said.
Little has been done since then and the situation remains critical, ALPA-SA told Reuters last week.

The International Federation of Airline Pilots Associations (IFALPA) in February classified the continent a high-risk area and said that collisions were only avoided by the skill of the pilots flying.
Statistics show that Africa has a crash rate of 14.9 per million flights, compared with 9.4 in South America, 1.3 in Asia and 0.7 in Europe and North America.

"It is true that pilots have coped with the situation so far. The question is for how long will they continue to do so. Those of us who regularly ply the African routes are fearful for our own safety, the safety of our aircraft and, most importantly, the safety of our passengers," said Van Heerden, now based in Singapore.
LAND AND AIR COMMUNICATION LINKS MISSING

Aviation associations say the most serious problem clouding African skies is a lack of communication between individual countries' air traffic control towers, as well as between those towers and the airplanes passing overhead.

"One of the great requirements is communication. Communication between countries and between the aircraft and the ground," said Gerry Coetzee, managing director of South Africa's Air Traffic Navigation and Services.

Van Heerden cited example after example of near-misses: pilots being given clearance for take-off and veering away from an incoming plane in the nick of time, not being warned of tailwinds, being directed to land on the same runway as another plane -- at the same time.
Coetzee says the solution to adequate communication lies in removing dependency from temperamental African land lines and making use of shared satellite communication.
He cites progress being made on the Very Small Apperture Terminal satellite system (VSAT), which would be able to relay communication on an aircraft's movements more reliably.
NEW SOUTH AFRICA RAISES RISK

The increase in the number of flights over Africa is mainly due to South Africa no longer being isolated from the rest of the world -- and particularly African states -- because of its apartheid regime, ALPA-SA said.
The country's democratic elections in April 1994 and the ensuing inauguration of Nelson Mandela as its first black president made South Africa an acceptable holiday and business destination.

Whereas planes to southern Africa previously had to detour around the bulge of Africa, they are now free to fly directly over the continent -- shortening the journey time but swelling the sky traffic faster than the infrastructure can handle.
"The upgrading of aeronautical facilities in many African states has not kept pace with the increase in traffic," said ALPA-SA general manager Cathy Bill.

"This has led to the fragility of the aviation infrastructure throughout a large part of the continent being highlighted and to a situation where the infrastructure cannot cope adequately with the large volumes of traffic," she said.
COUNTRIES GOVERN OWN AIRSPACE

While the International Civil Aviation Organisation (ICAO) and the United Nations agency responsible for civil aviation can adopt safety standards and make recommendations, each country governs its own airspace and is responsible for services.
Said ALPA-SA: "There is no absolute obligation on the part of a contracting state to comply with ICAO's requirements. There is no enforcement agency with the capability of demanding compliance."
